points.en: Every human being bears the image of God, so has a worth that is given by God, not earned, and cannot be revoked.
Irreducible: this worth is not reduced by age, size, usefulness or bodily or mental failure.
The world grants personhood on a sliding scale of capacities, but the church must see a person where the world sees a life not worth living.
Psalm 139 grounds worth in God, who formed and covered us in the womb, so life there is already His careful work.
Luke 1:41, the unborn John leaping for joy at Mary's greeting, shows a person responding to his Lord before birth.
Together they teach that worth comes from the Maker, not from capacities that develop later.
The unborn child's worth rests on the image of God, not on settling exactly when personhood begins.
Given uncertainty and the stakes of taking innocent life, the serious response is to err on the side of protecting life.
Hard cases such as a pregnancy truly threatening the mother's life differ morally from intending to kill the child, and must not excuse the whole.
The pastor who proclaims the sanctity of life must also proclaim the sufficiency of grace; no sin, including abortion, is beyond Christ's blood.
Like Jesus ('Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more'), the church joins conviction and pardon and is the safest place for the post-abortive.
Truth and compassion are not rivals but the two hands with which the shepherd lifts the fallen.
Euthanasia and assisted suicide, intentionally taking life to end suffering, are wrong because they usurp God's authority over life and death.
Allowing a dying patient to die by ceasing burdensome, futile treatment is not euthanasia but acceptance of mortality.
The older tradition: ordinary means of care are obligatory; excessively burdensome or hopeless extraordinary means may be declined.
Pain relief that may hasten death as a foreseen but unintended side effect is acceptable because the intent is to relieve suffering, not to kill.
At the bedside the pastor serves as a shepherd who prays and points to Christ who conquered death, not as a bioethicist reciting principles.
Dying well, committed into God's hands, is one of the last great works of the Christian life.
If every embryo is a person bearing God's image, procedures that create embryos to freeze, discard or destroy them are not morally neutral.
Third-party genetic material or surrogacy raise further questions to be weighed against the covenant, one-flesh nature of marriage.
The pastor begins with tenderness for the couple's pain, since the desire for children is good, yet does not wave away the questions.
The pastor must not out of sympathy dismiss questions about image-bearers' lives, nor out of zeal for principle coldly hand a rule to the grieving.
Truth and love belong together: never truth without love, never love that abandons truth.
The world ties personhood to capacities (thinking, choosing, contributing), so worth rises and falls with ability.
On that scale the very young, old, disabled and unconscious slide toward the margins as less than persons.
Scripture rejects it: worth is grounded in the Maker's image, which the weakest bear as fully as the strongest.
The steering conviction is that every human being bears the image of God.
Each is therefore owed protection and reverence, at life's beginning, its end and every fragile case between, including the defenseless and dying.
